In [[mathematics]], an '''analytic manifold''', also known as a <math>C^\omega</math> manifold, is a [[differentiable manifold]] with [[Analytic function|analytic]] transition maps.<ref name=":0">{{Citation|last=Varadarajan|first=V. S.|chapter=Differentiable and Analytic Manifolds|date=1984|title=Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Their Representations|pages=1–40|editor-last=Varadarajan|editor-first=V. S.|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics|volume=102|publisher=Springer|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-1126-6_1|isbn=978-1-4612-1126-6}}</ref> The term usually refers to real analytic manifolds, although [[complex manifold]]s are also analytic.<ref>{{citation|last=Vaughn|first=Michael T.|title=Introduction to Mathematical Physics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3Mnk63iqUc4C&pg=PA98|page=98|year=2008|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9783527618866}}.</ref> In algebraic geometry, [[analytic space]]s are a generalization of analytic manifolds such that singularities are permitted.

For <math>U \subseteq \R^n</math>, the space of analytic functions, <math>C^{\omega}(U)</math>, consists of infinitely differentiable functions <math>f:U \to \R </math>, such that the [[Taylor series]]

<math display=block>T_f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{|\alpha| \geq 0}\frac{D^\alpha f(\mathbf{x_0})}{\alpha!} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x_0})^\alpha</math>

converges to <math>f(\mathbf{x})</math> in a neighborhood of <math>\mathbf{x_0}</math>, for all <math>\mathbf{x_0} \in U</math>. The requirement that the transition maps be analytic is significantly more restrictive than that they be infinitely differentiable; the analytic manifolds are a proper subset of the [[Smoothness#Differentiability classes|smooth]], i.e. <math>C^\infty</math>, manifolds.<ref name=":0" /> There are many similarities between the theory of analytic and smooth manifolds, but a critical difference is that analytic manifolds do not admit analytic partitions of unity, whereas smooth [[Partition of unity|partitions of unity]] are an essential tool in the study of smooth manifolds.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Tu|first=Loring W.|title=An Introduction to Manifolds|title-link=An Introduction to Manifolds|date=2011|publisher=Springer New York|isbn=978-1-4419-7399-3|series=Universitext|location=New York, NY|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-7400-6}}</ref> A fuller description of the definitions and general theory can be found at [[differentiable manifold]]s, for the real case, and at [[complex manifold]]s, for the complex case.
